newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak PM says selloffs stand despite court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Slovak PM says selloffs stand despite court ruling.

text.p: The Slovak government on Friday said it would not overturn any direct sales of state property made by the National Property Fund (NPF) despite a court ruling that the law governing the sales was invalid.
Privatisation has been one of the hottest issues in Slovakia after a series of murky selloffs by the NPF which has dispersed state property totalling some 100 billion crowns in the last two years.

The Constitutional Court added fuel to the fire recently ruling that the government, and not the NPF, the state privatisation agency, was responsible for the direct sale of state property, contrary to a law adopted in November 1994.
The court ruling, which is not retroactive, prompted protests from some people in the ruling coalition and speculation in local media that some controversial NPF sell-off decisions might be reviewed.

"To those calling for a reversal of former acts of privatisation I say the government is ready to give its approval to all those decisions," Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar told Slovak radio in a regular interview.
In its ruling, the court said that the present law was unconstitutional on grounds that the constitution rules that the government is responsible for basic measures of economic and social policy.
Under the law, decisions on direct sales of state property were in the competence of the NPF. Previous to that law direct state selloffs were the government's responsibility.
"According to the law, we have six months to adopt some changes to the privatisation process, but it is impossible to subsequently analyse each and every sale," Meciar said.

The agency is currently run by supporters of Meciar's ruling coalition of his Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the ultra-right Slovak National Party (SDNS) and the ultra-left Workers' Party (ZRS), and is accused by the opposition of cronyism in direct sales to investors.
The current privatisation law was to have placed the NPF beyond the control of both the government and the anti-monopoly bureau.
This allowed arbitrary direct sales of state property even to undisclosed individuals at prices that sometimes were well below market value.
